passage:
Saturday
Dear Diary, it was Vijay's birthday party and I ate cake, two laddoos, green jelly and a whole packet of toffees. For one hour I was a rocket. I ran round the building three times and screamed on the swing. Then at six I felt like a flat balloon. My head hurt, I shouted at Vijay when he wanted the swing, and I cried because my shoe was tied wrong. Mummy didn't say "no more sweets ever". She gave me dal-rice and curd for dinner and said tomorrow the sweets can come after lunch, not instead of it. I felt better after eating. I said sorry to Vijay on the phone.
Reena

qa.q: What did Mummy give Reena for dinner?
qa.a: Mummy gave Reena dal-rice and curd.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling at six o'clock, and what shows it?
qa.a: Reena felt tired and irritable, like a flat balloon; the headache, shouting at Vijay and crying over a shoe show it.

qa.q: What was sensible about Mummy's plan for sweets?
qa.a: Instead of banning sweets, Mummy kept them for after a proper meal, which keeps energy and mood steadier.

qa.q: How might Vijay have felt when Reena shouted at him on his birthday?
qa.a: Vijay was probably hurt and confused, since he only wanted a turn on the swing at his own party.

grounding: Illustrates a child going hyper after sweets and then irritable and tired, with a balanced meal and treats after food keeping mood steadier than a ban.

passage:
Wednesday night.
Third day this week I skipped breakfast so I could sleep twenty extra minutes. By second period my head felt full of cotton. In maths Anjali asked me to pass the compass and I snapped, "Take it yourself." She looked at me like I'd slapped her. At eleven I read the same line of the chemistry notes four times and it still meant nothing. My stomach growled so loudly in the test that the boy behind me laughed. At lunch I ate everything and felt normal again, almost silly for how grumpy I'd been. Tonight I asked Ma to wake me at 6:40 and I've put a banana and a box of poha on the table myself. Easier than being a monster by noon. Need to say sorry to Anjali tomorrow.
Arnab

qa.q: How many times did Arnab read the same line of the chemistry notes?
qa.a: Arnab read the same line four times.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel after eating lunch?
qa.a: Arnab felt normal again, and a bit sheepish about being so grumpy all morning.

qa.q: What small step has Arnab taken to avoid the noon crash?
qa.a: Arnab asked Ma for a 6:40 wake-up and set out a banana and some poha, a simple breakfast that fits the morning.

qa.q: What might Anjali have thought when Arnab snapped at her?
qa.a: Anjali was probably hurt and surprised, since she only asked for a compass and got a rude reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager who skips breakfast to sleep longer feeling foggy, moody and unable to concentrate before lunch, then planning a simple regular breakfast.

passage:
I teach Class 10 here, so I see the lunch hour every day. Since the term began, Naveen has been opening his tiffin, rearranging the chapati and closing it again. He carries a small notebook that he snaps shut when anyone passes. On Monday a boy joked loudly about Naveen's "new skinny look" and a few laughed. I didn't know what was going on inside him, and I still don't. But I stopped the joke on the spot, without making Naveen the topic, and later asked him to help me carry books to the staffroom. There I said only that I had noticed lunch seemed hard lately and that I cared. He shrugged, eyes wet. That evening I phoned his parents, gently, and suggested a visit to their family doctor.
Irawati, class teacher

qa.q: What does Naveen do with his tiffin at lunch?
qa.a: He has been opening his tiffin, rearranging the chapati and closing it again.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after the joke at lunch, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Irawati was worried and protective; the teacher stopped the joke at once and then made a private chance to show care.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's private approach wiser than raising it in class?
qa.a: A quiet word and a call to the parents avoided shaming Naveen in public, and the doctor's visit brings in the right help.

qa.q: How might Naveen have experienced the teacher's words in the staffroom?
qa.a: He may have felt exposed but also noticed and cared for; he shrugged, but his eyes were wet.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a teenager becoming secretive and anxious about eating, stopping public body comments and choosing private concern and a doctor's advice.

Subject: hostel update (not dramatic, promise)

Hi Gautam bhaiya,
You asked why I sounded half-asleep on Sunday's call. Honest answer: I've been living on instant noodles, chips from the vending machine and 1 a.m. bread-omelette from the gate stall. By afternoon lectures I'm yawning, and I skipped Saturday badminton because I just couldn't be bothered. I felt low and didn't know why. Then my roommate put a bowl of curd and a banana in front of me at breakfast and said, "Try this for a week." It's been six days. I'm not eating perfectly, but I now take dal and rice at the mess at lunch and keep fruit in my cupboard. I feel less foggy in the labs. Don't tell Amma about the noodles, okay?
Jahnavi

qa.q: What did the roommate put in front of Jahnavi at breakfast?
qa.a: A bowl of curd and a banana.

qa.q: How was Jahnavi feeling before the changes, and what shows it?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt low, tired and unmotivated, yawning through lectures and skipping Saturday badminton.

qa.q: Why do small upgrades work better for Jahnavi than a perfect diet?
qa.a: Adding dal, rice, fruit and curd is easy to keep up in a hostel, so Jahnavi feels better without changing everything at once.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel reading this email?
qa.a: Gautam would likely feel relieved and a little amused, glad to know why Jahnavi sounded half-asleep and that things are improving.

grounding: Shows a young adult living on instant snacks and late-night food feeling tired and low, and small additions like curd, fruit and dal helping without a perfect diet.

"Just one pull," Preeti said, holding out the vape behind the tuition centre. "It tastes like mango. Everyone's tried it."
The others were watching. Pankaj felt his ears go hot.
"Nah, I'm good."
"Scared?"
"Bit, honestly." He shrugged. "My cousin started with 'just one' in Class 9. Now he can't sit through a movie without going outside for it. And our science sir said it messes with your brain while it's still growing."
"You sound like a poster."
"Fine, I sound like a poster." He grinned. "Samosa at the corner stall?"
Preeti rolled her eyes, but she slipped the vape back into her bag. "You're paying."
"Obviously."

passage: Uma, you asked why I look like a zombie, so here's the story. Board prep week, right? I'm Ritu, the girl who thinks she can beat biology in five nights. So I bought those tall energy drinks from the corner shop, a couple every night, and studied till three. First night I felt like a superhero. Second night my hands were shaking over the diagram of the heart, my own heart was thumping, and I couldn't sleep even when I lay down at four. Next morning I blanked on a question I knew. Then I panicked, drank another can, and the whole thing repeated. On Friday Papa found three cans in my bin and sat with me instead of shouting. Now it's lights off by eleven-thirty, a proper dinner, and a short walk between chapters. My hands are steady again, Uma.

passage: Gopika, you're off to that farewell party tonight, so let your Urmila Bua tell you something from when I was twenty. College fest, a friend's rooftop, and someone kept filling my cup. A boy from the next flat asked us to turn the music down, and I was sure he was joking, so I turned it up. The counselling room at the college smelled of old files and tea. Baljeet sat on the edge of the chair, twisting a hostel key.
"It's my brother, Ramesh. He's drinking every night now. Last weekend he took the money I'd saved for books and didn't come home."
"How are you sleeping?" the counsellor asked.
"Badly. I keep my phone loud in case Mummy calls. I'm angry with him, and then ashamed of being angry. And tired. So tired."
"You can't make Ramesh stop. That part isn't yours to carry. But you can decide what you will and won't do."
Baljeet was quiet. "No more lending him anything. And I'll stop answering his calls after midnight."
"That's a fair limit. There's also a family support group here on Thursdays. Would you try one meeting?"
Baljeet nodded slowly.

qa.q: When does the family support group meet?
qa.a: On Thursdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Baljeet describe, and what shows the strain?
qa.a: Baljeet feels angry, then ashamed of the anger, and deeply tired; the twisted key and sleepless nights with a loud phone show the strain.

qa.q: What limits does Baljeet choose, and why are they wise?
qa.a: No more lending and no calls after midnight; they protect Baljeet without pretending to control Ramesh.

qa.q: How might Mummy be affected by Ramesh's drinking, judging from the passage?
qa.a: Mummy is probably worried too, since Baljeet keeps the phone loud in case she calls.

grounding: Shows a young adult affected by a brother's growing drinking feeling worry, anger, shame and exhaustion, and choosing limits and support instead of control.
